summary: Both sides draw the same white lightning bolt — a zap that starts at pixel 0 and jumps rightward in random-width chunks to pixel 59, each chunk flashing at full 255 and fading out behind it, then a dark pause before the next zap — with statistically indistinguishable zap rate, step timing, segment widths and traverse time; the port's only visible difference is a slightly slower fade that leaves a ~25% longer/brighter tail.
observations: Structure (identical on both): a single 'zap' propagates left-to-right. Each step lights a fresh contiguous segment at pure white 255,255,255 (no colour at all — every dumped pixel has R=G=B on both sides), and the previously lit segment fades. Every zap in 20 s of dumped frames starts at pixel 0 and its last segment ends at pixel 59, on both sides — no reversed, mid-strip or partial zaps on either.

Zap rate (default rig, 60 px, 20 fps, seed 1, 400 dumped frames): orig 11 zaps in 20 s (0.55/s), port 11 zaps in 20 s (0.55/s). Confirmed over longer windows: 120 s @20 fps mean brightness orig 8.3 / port 10.3, and across seeds 1/7/1234 orig 8.3-8.4 vs port 9.3-10.6.
Traverse time per zap (20 fps): orig avg 1.05 s (median 0.95, max 2.05); port avg 1.16 s (median 1.15, max 2.00). Dark gap between zaps: orig avg 0.82 s (0.40-1.25); port avg 0.71 s (0.40-1.00).

Step cadence within a zap (20 fps, frames between consecutive segment onsets): orig histogram {1:20, 2:19, 3:11, 4:10, 5:11, 6:3, 7:4}, avg 2.97 frames; port {1:30, 2:18, 3:12, 4:8, 5:9, 6:3, 7:5, 8:3}, avg 2.91 frames. Same shape, same mean — the port's random step delay matches.

Segment width (20 fps dump): orig avg 7.01 px, range 2-10, mass concentrated 5-10; port avg 6.67 px, range 1-10, with a few 1 px and more 4 px segments. Segments per zap: orig 8.1, port 9.0. Minor: the port's width distribution reaches ~1-2 px lower than the original's.

Fade rate is the one real difference. Per-pixel decay after a 255 flash at 20 fps: orig 255 -> 63 -> 15 -> 3 -> 0 (4 lit frames, 0.20 s); port 255 -> 101 -> 39 -> 14 -> 4 -> 0 (5 lit frames, 0.25 s). At 40 fps: orig 255,159,99,62,38,24,15,9,5,3,2,1 and port 255,177,123,85,58,40,27,17,11,7,3,1 — both 12 frames / 0.30 s, but the port's curve sits consistently above the original's. Net effect: port mean brightness runs ~20-25% higher and lit-frame fraction 0.66 vs 0.50 over 120 s at 20 fps.

Both sides are frame-rate coupled in the same way (decay factor looks like 1 - k*dt on both, with k ~= 15/s on the original and ~= 12/s on the port), so at 40 fps they agree closely and at 20 fps they differ only by the extra tail frame above.

Below ~15 fps both degenerate, but DIFFERENTLY. At 10 fps the original's decay factor goes negative and the pixel alternates 255,0,63,0,15,0,3,0 — a strobing afterglow that still reads as a fading trail (lit-frame fraction 0.73, mean 14.8 over 240 s); the port instead clips to zero and shows bare single-frame flashes with no trail at all (lit fraction 0.39, mean 11.1). At 5 fps the original blows up completely — segments never die, the strip fills to nearly all-white (survey mean brightness 147/255) — while the port stays sparse (mean 19). Note this regime is the ORIGINAL's own arithmetic breaking down, not a sane look either side reproduces.

No controls on either side: meta.json lists an empty control list for orig and port, and --probe-controls reports '(no settable controls)' for both. Neither side binds sensor globals (wantsSensors false on both).

No runtime or compile errors on either side in any run; no drift or death — 120 s at 20 fps and a --skip 100 late window both look identical in character to t=0 on both sides, and three well-separated seeds (1, 7, 1234) give the same statistics.

The 60 s / 5 fps standard survey is misleading for this pattern (orig mean 147 vs port 19) purely because of the sub-15-fps blow-up above; the 240 s / 10 fps and 120 s / 20 fps surveys show a uniform stochastic zap stream with no mode or regime structure on either side.
feedback: Only substantive fix: the port's afterglow fades too slowly. Measured decay factor per frame is ~ (1 - 12*dt) against the original's ~ (1 - 15*dt). At 20 fps that is orig 255->63->15->3 (4 lit frames) versus port 255->101->39->14->4 (5 lit frames), and it lifts the port's mean brightness ~20-25% and its lit-frame fraction from 0.50 to 0.66. Speeding the fade by ~25% would make the two indistinguishable at 20-40 fps.

Minor: the port occasionally emits 1-3 px segments (4 of width 1 in a 99-segment sample) where the original's minimum practical width is ~5 px (only one segment each of width 2, 3, 4 in 89 samples). Raising the port's minimum step width to ~5 px would tighten the match.

Minor: the port's dark gap between zaps averages 0.71 s against the original's 0.82 s, and it uses ~9 segments per zap against the original's ~8. Both are within seed noise at n=11 zaps, but if a fixer touches the timing, nudge the inter-zap pause slightly longer.

Low priority / optional: below ~15 fps the two diverge sharply because the original lets its decay factor go negative (pixels alternate 255,0,63,0,... at 10 fps and the strip saturates to near-white at 5 fps) while the port clamps to zero (single-frame flashes, no trail). Reproducing the original's blow-up is probably not worth it, but the port drops the trail entirely at 10 fps where the original still shows one, so if low-frame-rate fidelity matters, make the fade time-based rather than letting the linear factor clip.
